{< include ../exercise-header.qmd >}


::: {#exr-falcon-show-mug}
We can experiment with this idea using the computer. Since we are going to be trying out different proposals for small, it helps to give a name to the increment in input being used. We will call it `h`. In the following chunk, we have set `h <- 0.2`, matching the situation shown in @fig-f-of-t. We will calculate the rate of change in two different ways: one using the value of `h`, the other using an smaller value, say, `h/10`. In both cases, we calculate the change in the output divided by the change in the input.

::: {.content-include unless-format="html"}
```{webr}
#| context: setup
#| autorun: true
#| echo: false
raw <- mosaicCalc::doodle_fun(~ t, seed = 937)
f <- makeFun((raw((t-2.5)*2 ) + 10)/2 ~ t)
```

```{webr}
h <- 0.2
(f(3 + h) - f(3)) / (h)  # "small"
(f(3 + h/10) - f(3)) / (h/10) # smaller
```
:::

::: {.content-include unless-format="pdf"}
The following R statements calculate the rate of change of the function $f(t)$ for input $t=3$.


```{r}
#| label: ch14-r-1dcb1f93
#| echo: false
raw <- mosaicCalc::doodle_fun(~ t, seed = 937)
f <- makeFun((raw((t-2.5)*2 ) + 10)/2 ~ t)
```

```{r}
#| label: ch14-r-ca3bba41
h <- 0.2
(f(3 + h) - f(3)) / (h)  # "small"
(f(3 + h/10) - f(3)) / (h/10) # smaller
```
:::

When `h <- 0.2`, the "small" calculation and the "smaller" calculation give discernibly different results. This means that 0.2 is *not* a small value for `h`, or at least is not small enough to meet the second criterion.

::: {.content-include unless-format="html"}
We can search for "small enough" `h`. Run the above chunk with a smaller starting `h`, say `h <- 0.01`. If that's not small enough, try even smaller: `h <- 0.001`. Continue, as needed, until the "small" and "smaller" rates of change are not discernibly different.
:::

::: {.content-include unless-format="pdf"}
We can search for "small enough" `h`. Let's try $h = 0.001$.

```{r}
#| label: ch14-r-a0703d37
# Try a smaller h
h <- 0.001
(f(3 + h) - f(3)) / (h)  # even smaller
(f(3 + h/10) - f(3)) / (h/10) # smaller still
```

Now the rates of change for $h=0.001$ and $h = 0.0001$ are virtually the same. Using even smaller values for $h$ would give even closer results.  
:::

:::
